newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Miners say Indonesian rules could harm investment.
newsitem.headline: Miners say Indonesian rules could harm investment.

text.p: Indonesia has proposed sweeping changes to its mining regulations with a nationalistic flavour, which industry sources said on Thursday could dampen the investment climate.
The proposals are in the form of amendments to the seventh-generation contracts of work (COW), which were approved in principle last year and accepted by mining companies.

The new regulations follow the Busang gold scandal, in which prominent Indonesians scrambled for a share of the action before an independent auditor revealed it to be the biggest scam in mining history.
But there appeared to be confusion within the government itself over the proposals.
State Secretary Murdiono said the government would be consistent with its mining rules that allow 100-percent foreign owned companies to operate in the sector.
"Who said it is compulsory," he said when asked about a proposed 10 percent stake to be given to the government. "If it is an idea it's okay, but we must implement the rules."
Investment Minister Sanyoto Sastrowardoyo said: "It is a new thing. I don't know what the reasons are or the motivation."
Mining and diplomatic analysts said this appeared to leave the proposals up in the air. Some foreign mining officials called for a united front against the new rules.
M. Simatupang, vice-chairman of the Indonesian Mining Association (IMA), said foreign companies had been given until next Tuesday to indicate if they wanted to negotiate.
"Foreign mining companies which had applied for the COW were very concerned over the proposed changes, especially because the COW had been given approval in principle," he told Reuters.

"The companies are in a crisis. The companies were initially told to take it or leave it, but the director-general of mining has since told the IMA it's up to the companies to negotiate... to accept or whatever," he said.
Coal mining companies were called in on Thursday for a briefing on the first contracts of work to cover the coal industry and bring it in line with mineral mining.

The mining proposals include a free 10 percent share in a project, which could increase depending on the project's viability, an offer of shares to cooperatives or a company owned by a regional government, and training programmes to ensure that Indonesians occupy all posts below the level of director by the sixth year of operation.
The new regulations also call for an allocation of capital gains made on a stock exchange outside Indonesia to shareholders in a company in proportion to their equity.

If the company wishes to obtain additional capital by making a public offering, the offering must be done on the Indonesian stock exchange. A public offering of the company, however, may be made outside Indonesia.
No data should be made public without consent of the government. Such data should be evaluated by a third party consultant which has been appointed by the company with government approval.
"This could jeopardise the whole climate for investment here," a senior foreign mining source said. "It certainly could cause a whole new re-think on Indonesia as an area to invest in," he said.
"The proposals are hard to follow," another senior foreign mining executive said. "They are not practical or desirable."

"The whole advantage of the COW system is fixing the rules of the game for the future. Mining is a very capital intensive, long-term business not like a shoe factory where there's a relatively fast payout of the capital investment," he said.
He said the proposals could dent the investment climate and smacked of rising nationalism after the Busang incident.

Canadian mining company Bre-X Minerals Ltd declared that Busang contained 71 million ounces of gold, making it the biggest find this century, but an independent audit found the property nearly worthless and the data falsified.
